past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (well controlled on insulin pump)
No prior neuromuscular or autoimmune disease besides DM1

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented. Normal cognition and language.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, right greater than left. Levator excursion right 6mm, left 10mm. Complete fatigable ptosis right eye on sustained upgaze at 38 seconds. Horizontal diplopia on leftward gaze. Right eye adduction weakness. Pupils equal, reactive. No proptosis. Facial weakness bilateral.
neurological_exam.motor: Deltoids 4-/5. Hip flexors 4/5. Neck flexors 4-/5. Distal 5/5. Clear fatigability on sustained arm elevation and neck flexion.
neurological_exam.additional: Voice nasal after 3 minutes speech. Mild dysphagia — pills difficult to swallow. NIF -60 cmH2O. No respiratory distress. Patient noted: as a pharmacist she recognized fatigability as potentially NMJ-related and specifically requested MG workup.

patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and swallowing difficulty for 10 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: A 45-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus managed with an insulin pump presented with 10 weeks of bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia. She works as a pharmacist and described noticing her right eyelid drooping approximately 10 weeks ago. She recognized the diurnal variation (consistently worse at the end of her 10-hour pharmacy shifts, better after a night's sleep) as potentially significant and began researching myasthenia gravis. She developed horizontal double vision on looking to the left approximately 7 weeks ago, with the images side by side and worsening with sustained left lateral gaze. She has had difficulty swallowing pills over the past 4 weeks — she has to swallow each pill separately with a large quantity of water and cannot take the multiple tablets she used to take all at once. She reports that her voice becomes nasal and that patients at the pharmacy have commented that her speech sounds different in the afternoon. She has had proximal arm weakness — she asked her colleague to help her reach upper pharmacy shelves because her arms tire out overhead. She denies sensory symptoms, no headache, no neck pain, no limb weakness at rest. Her type 1 diabetes is very well controlled with her insulin pump (HbA1c 6.6%). She specifically requested that her primary care physician order anti-AChR antibodies, which came back from outside laboratory as 'reported as borderline positive.' She was then referred urgently to neurology. Her family history includes paternal type 1 diabetes; she was not aware of MG in her family. She has not had any recent infections, new medications, or stressful events beyond her normal busy work schedule.

findings.result: Marked improvement in ptosis within 60 seconds of edrophonium — ptosis reduced from complete to minimal
findings.significance: Positive pharmacological response — marked improvement in ptosis following edrophonium administration
Normal motor and sensory conduction; normal baseline CMAP amplitudes

specialized_test.impression: Clearly abnormal RNS with 17–20% decremental responses at deltoid and nasalis. Positive edrophonium (Tensilon) test with marked improvement in ptosis. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 5.8 nmol/L (reference <0.5 nmol/L). Anti-AChR blocking and modulating antibodies also elevated. Anti-MuSK negative. Anti-titin negative. Anti-GAD65 antibody markedly elevated (>2000 IU/mL; reference <5 IU/mL). Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; elevated results are associated with autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease. Clinical correlation recommended.
abnormal_values_summary: Anti-AChR binding 5.8 nmol/L (markedly elevated; ref <0.5 nmol/L)

findings.description: No anterior mediastinal mass. Residual thymic tissue with fatty involution appropriate for age 45. No lymphadenopathy. No thymoma identified.

ct.impression: No anterior mediastinal mass identified. Residual thymic tissue with fatty involution appropriate for age. No lymphadenopathy. Lungs clear. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG with increased jitter (mean MCD 71 µs) and high blocking rate (75%). Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: Prednisone 15-20mg daily for MG in Type 1 diabetic on insulin pump
interactions: Prednisone + insulin pump: corticosteroids cause significant insulin resistance and hyperglycemia — pump settings will need adjustment
Expected glucose impact: typically requires 20-50% increase in basal rate and correction bolus increases
warnings: Consult endocrinology for insulin pump adjustment protocol during corticosteroid initiation
Patient (pharmacist) may already have understanding of this interaction — engage her knowledge
Start glucose monitoring 4x daily minimum during steroid initiation
Steroid-induced hyperglycemia typically peaks 4-8 hours after prednisone dose
alternatives: Azathioprine as steroid-sparing to minimize prednisone exposure in T1DM

warnings: Codeine allergy (nausea) does not contraindicate pyridostigmine
Warn patient of GI side effects of pyridostigmine — nausea, cramping; start low (30-45mg q6h) and titrate
Glycopyrrolate 1mg TID may reduce cholinergic GI side effects if needed

output.query: Thymectomy myasthenia gravis MGTX trial non-thymomatous AChR positive

results.title: MGTX Trial: Randomized Thymectomy in Myasthenia Gravis
results.finding: Thymectomy + prednisone superior to prednisone alone in AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; lower QMG scores, lower prednisone requirements, higher remission rates at 3 years; thymectomy recommended regardless of CT chest

results.title: Laparoscopic vs robotic thymectomy for MG
results.finding: VATS and robotic approaches have equivalent outcomes to median sternotomy for non-invasive thymoma and thymic hyperplasia; shorter hospital stay, less pain

output.summary: MGTX trial (NEJM 2016) provides Class I evidence that thymectomy + prednisone is superior to prednisone alone in AChR antibody-positive generalized neuromuscular junction disease aged 18–65, regardless of CT chest findings. VATS and robotic approaches have equivalent outcomes to median sternotomy for non-invasive thymic pathology with shorter hospital stay.

critical_actions: Anti-AChR antibodies clearly confirm MG — no ambiguity

contraindicated_actions: Do NOT attribute fatigable ptosis to diabetic cranial mononeuropathy — DM CN palsy is non-fatigable and acute in onset
Do NOT use mycophenolate in reproductive-age woman
Do NOT start prednisone without endocrinology guidance in T1DM on insulin pump
key_reasoning_points: Type 1 diabetes with anti-GAD65 antibodies is a polyautoimmunity context — MG is a second autoimmune disorder
Diabetic cranial neuropathy (CN3, CN6) is non-fatigable — fatigable bilateral ptosis identifies NMJ disorder
Patient's pharmacy background led to self-diagnosis and appropriate care-seeking — initial 'borderline positive' AChR at outside lab was actually significant
Insulin pump adjustment is mandatory when starting corticosteroids — steroids cause significant insulin resistance in T1DM

red_herrings.data_point: Type 1 diabetes mellitus — concern for diabetic cranial neuropathy
